parts: House and home; functions of a home

A house is a physical construction of brick, sand, cement and stone; it becomes a home when family members live there and carry out health, ease, comfort, social and entertainment activities. A home has protective (security, protection from weather, animals and enemies), economic (value in money, raises socio-economic status, gives pride, can host income-generating activity such as tuitions or a paying guest), educative (basic values, life skills such as sharing and caring) and social/religious functions (interaction within and outside the family, belongingness, passing values and customs down the generations; celebrating festivals).

The site is the place where a house is built. Consider: neighbourhood – a developed area with electricity, roads and drainage and nearby post office, bank, school and market; physical features – open area, away from heavy traffic (air and noise pollution), avoid low-lying land (flooding and water-logging), elevated sites give a better view and drain water; soil – firm 2–5 feet below the surface for a strong foundation, loose soil makes the house tilt, sandy and gravelly soils make it hot, rocky surface is good for foundation but does not absorb water and complicates laying drainage pipes; sanitary requirements – avoid garbage-filled plots (uneven level, drainage problems), fill with fresh firm soil and raise to road level; practical convenience – market, transport, post office, bank and hospital within reasonable walking distance.

Make a list of activities in each room and mark space for each; combine activities (dining with kitchen or drawing room, study with bedroom); do not overcrowd; use multipurpose furniture (sofa-cum-bed, dining table for study), furniture as room dividers and storage, space under the staircase for a store or toilet. Living room: for entertaining guests, relaxation and reading; near the entrance; furniture arranged so that people can talk; good lighting. Bedroom: privacy, free from noise, rectangular shape is convenient, preferably attached to a bathroom (we spend about one-third of life sleeping). Bathroom: bathing space, water closet and wash area; non-slippery, easy-to-clean floor; at least one wall exposed to the outside for light and air. Kitchen: ideally in the east or north-east to get morning sunlight (a disinfectant), good drainage, wire-mesh doors, adequate day and night lighting, one wall on the exterior, exhaust fan, cross ventilation, storage above and below the counter, light-coloured walls.

Natural light (sun) is important for all rooms, especially kitchen and bathrooms; without sun they stay dark and damp, attract mosquitoes and cockroaches and increase infections and fungal diseases. Artificial light should fall on the work, not in the eyes; glare causes eye ache. Ventilation circulates fresh air and drives out stale air through windows, ventilators and exhaust fans; keep at least one window open even in winter; cross ventilation by windows on two sides or a door and window opposite each other; openings at floor level bring in fresh air and those near the ceiling drive out stale air. Sanitation covers cleanliness, removal of garbage and disposal of waste water and excreta.

Cleaning is daily (sweeping, mopping, dusting, making beds, tidying, cleaning rugs), weekly (bathrooms, toilets, washbasins, cobwebs, shelves, door handles, polishing wood) and seasonal or spring cleaning (airing mattresses, washing curtains, cleaning the store room and woodwork, thorough cleaning before Diwali). Start daily cleaning from the innermost part after making beds, open windows, sweep with a soft broom, dust, brush carpets and mop with phenyl. Use indoor footwear and foot mats; fine wire mesh keeps out dust and insects. Materials: floors – broom, soap, kerosene, phenyl; tiles – soap, vinegar, mild hydrochloric acid; plastic buckets and mugs – lukewarm soap solution, vinegar, soda (no hard cleaners); glass and mirrors – moist newspaper, vinegar; metal and brass taps – lemon, vinegar, tamarind, salt; wood – soft cloth wrung from mild soap solution.

Garbage: collect in a covered dustbin, empty daily into the public bin; segregate bio-degradable (peels) from non-bio-degradable (plastic); in villages bury bio-degradable waste in a pit to make manure. Waste water goes by drain to a kitchen garden or soakage pit, never left to stagnate. Soakage pit: about 2 m deep, 1 m wide and 2–3 m long, one-third filled with coarse stones, then small stones and pebbles, then sand, covered with earth and grass; not built near a well; needs no drainage system. Human excreta: water closet (most sanitary, needs plenty of water and is expensive); septic tank (Sulabh Shauchalaya; hygienic, low cost, no pollution of surface or ground water, no foul smell, needs only 1.5–2 litres of water for flushing against 13–14 litres in a flush toilet, no cleaning of pits, sludge is good manure, prevents mosquitoes and flies); pit latrine (more than 3 m deep, sandy soil, covered; temporary use, can pollute ground water).
